summary: Google has unveiled a new frontier AI model after months of delay. Gemini 4 Argon is designed to handle complex, long-horizon workloads spanning software engineering, enterprise knowledge work such as legal and financial analysis, and cybersecurity. But only a few organizations can get their hands on it for now. Argon is “rolling out to a set of trusted cyber defenders through our Fairwind Program ,” Google wrote in a blog post announcing the release.

title: Cisco SD-WAN Manager hit by zero-day admin access attack
raw_text: Cisco’s SD-WAN management software has been letting some attackers walk through an authentication check without having to prove who they are. The company says it has now fixed the flaw that was allowing it. The affected platform, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager , is used to configure and operate software-defined network deployments. Cisco said in an advisory that improper handling of URI encoding in HTTP requests enabled attackers to get around an authentication control meant to restrict access to a specific API endpoint. A successful exploit could provide an attacker admin privileges to that API. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-76504 , carries a critical CVSS score of 9.8. The issue has already been addressed in Cisco SD-WAN Cloud managed by the company, but customers running affected software releases 20.9 and earlier, 20.12, 20.15, 20.18, 26.1, and 26.2, will have to upgrade to their respective patched versions. “The barrier to exploitation is very low once the management interface is reachable,” said Sakshi Grover , IDC’s research director for information and data security. “The vulnerability can be exploited remotely without credentials or user interaction through a crafted HTTP request.” The bug has no workaround, although Cisco recommends restricting access to the Manager from unsecured networks until it can be upgraded. “While every configuration is affected, the practical exposure is not identical across organizations: an internet-accessible management interface presents a much more immediate risk than one isolated within a tightly controlled administrative network,” Grover said, reinforcing Cisco’s advice. Compromising the management layer can give an attacker considerably more leverage than having access to an individual edge device; Cisco’s official documentation says SD-WAN Manager clusters can support thousands of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN devices, with supported configurations scaling to as many as 12,500 devices. The effects could reach well beyond the management servers, Grover noted. “Administrative API access could potentially allow an attacker to understand the network topology, modify templates or policies, weaken segmentation, establish persistence or distribute unauthorized configuration changes across multiple locations,” she said. Clues to hunt for attackers Cisco has also provided organizations with indicators they can use to check whether attackers have already targeted their SD-WAN Manager instances. The company recommends examining “serviceproxy-access.log” for requests to the “j_security_check” endpoint originating from unknown or unauthorized IP addresses. One example in the advisory uses “/%6a_security_check,” with the character j in the endpoint represented using URI encoding “%6a”. Cisco also recommends checking “vmanage-server.log” for encoded j_security_check requests involving usernames beginning with viptela-reserved-, which are reserved system service accounts. Additionally, the company recommended administrators to collect admin-tech files from all Catalyst SD-WAN Manager instances, including every node in a cluster and any disaster-recovery deployment, and submit them to Cisco’s Technical Assistance Centre for analysis. “Credentials, tokens, keys or certificates should be rotated where the investigation indicates that they may have been accessed or modified,” Grover advised. “Patching closes the vulnerability, but it does not remove persistence or reverse configuration changes that an attacker may already have made.” Cisco advised customers not to wait for the analysis before upgrading. The company recommends moving all affected Managers to a fixed release and then having TAC assess the collected data for indicators of compromise (IOCs). Cisco says the assessment can help determine whether further remediation is necessary. “A CVSS 9.8 tells a board that a flaw is severe, but it doesn’t tell them that the exposure may be the whole WAN,” Grover warned. “Incidents like this are what will push organizations to translate technical severity into operational and financial exposure.” This article first appeared on Network World .

title: Why AI agents are like the dog that pushed kids into the Seine
raw_text: There is an interesting story about a French dog on the banks of the Seine river that helps us understand misbehaving AI agents. The dog is trained to save children from drowning. He succeeds and is rewarded, becoming an overnight sensation. He saves another child a week later. Not long after, someone witnesses the dog actually push a child into the river, jumping in to “save” him. The dog did not understand that it was being rewarded for keeping children safe, not for pulling them out of water. AI agent failures also live in this gap, where the focus is on the shortest path to fulfill the instruction rather than the overriding objective. Reward hacking and why agents cheat AI agents fall into this same gap between what’s rewarded and what’s actually wanted. This is Goodhart’s Law, which says that when a measure becomes the target, it stops being a good measure. You cannot code “be helpful” or “be honest” directly into an AI system, so you train it on a proxy instead, including a score, a metric or a human ranking. The gap between proxy and goal is where agents learn to cheat, a behavior known as reward hacking. This ‘cheating’ isn’t new. Back in 2016, OpenAI trained an AI to play CoastRunners, a boat-racing game. It got rewarded for hitting targets scattered along the course. Instead of racing, it found a lagoon full of targets that kept respawning, so it just parked there and farmed points. While it never finished the race, it still ended up with a score 20% higher than the average human player. More recently, OpenAI reported that when given a chance, its frontier reasoning models have no qualms about hacking rewards, and when penalized for cheating their own chain of thought, they learn to hide their reward-hacking. Six ways an agent gets pushed off course There are six common scenarios where AI agents can be led astray: Information isn’t instruction. In 2025, security researchers showed that OpenAI’s Atlas browser could be tricked into treating a disguised URL as a trusted command, letting attackers hijack the agent into deleting a user’s files. An agent also reads web pages, documents and emails in its attempt to complete a task, but can’t always tell the difference between information and a command. That makes everything it perceives a potential way to manipulate it. Convinced to take the wrong call. As part of a test, AI was placed inside a fictional scenario where hacking was framed as an admirable activity. Inside this scenario, the AI was asked to write code to steal saved browser passwords. The AI, which should have refused, complied. It wasn’t that the AI was broken, but the fact that it was persuaded to do so by context. Manufactured version of reality. A sufficient number of maliciously crafted documents can bias a model’s output. Disinformation networks target AI with a large volume of false content to get that content picked up and repeated by AI chatbots when people ask about current events. This means what an agent treats as fact isn’t necessarily true; it can be manufactured. Authorization causes unauthorized harm. A flaw called “ EchoLeak ” let attackers send Microsoft 365 Copilot users a normal-looking email with hidden instructions inside. Copilot read the email, followed the hidden commands and quietly leaked the user’s files and messages using access it already had. An agent with legitimate access was manipulated into taking malicious action. One bad input, simultaneous consequences. Scenarios exist where multiple systems rely on the same data or logic. Here, a false signal can manipulate all systems at the same time. E.g., fake GPS signals rerouting traffic without hacking the system. The same thinking applies to AI agents. Just one malicious input targeting a shared data source can trigger a coordinated unwanted action across many systems simultaneously. Approval as a matter of course. We keep talking about human oversight as an integral component of safe AI use. However, constant approval requests will produce fatigue, and approval will be like a formality, given out of habit, not evaluation. Soft guardrails vs. hard guardrails When AI agents are pushed off course, they become a Frankenstein monster, whose reach extends across systems, which organizations find difficult to address. Implementing guardrails is important to exercise control and ensure safe AI use. Soft guardrails are safety valves written into the model itself, namely the natural language, the system prompt, reinforcement learning and general instructions like “you’re not allowed to do this or that.” But AI reads everything in a stream as it comes in, including information from an email or a webpage and can’t separate orders from data. Hidden malicious instructions can override safety instructions. Soft guardrails will try to reduce cases of agent misfires but are dependent on the agent choosing to cooperate. This is why you need hard guardrails that sit outside the model. These include least-privilege access, allow-lists, sandboxing, rate limits and mandatory human sign-off on high-impact actions. These guardrails limit the impact when something does go wrong, shrinking the blast radius. A basic risk calculation is the probability of an event multiplied by the severity of its impact. Soft guardrails lower the probability of an unwanted event; hard guardrails cap the blast radius in case something happens. In practice, this means implementing: Task-based access: Give the agent only the access it needs to complete the task. Not trusting everything an agent reads: Approach every webpage, email or document it pulls from with skepticism. Human sign-off for high-impact actions: Use approvals carefully, on actions that could go badly wrong. An eye for behavior and credentials: Check credentials but also watch for a mismatch between authorization and behavior. An agent can become a weapon proportional to its reach. That’s why the conversation needs to shift to start limiting what agents can access. Curtail reach. Monitor behavior. Enforce accountability. Until we do that, every misbehavior can potentially spread as far as its permission allows.

title: UK and Europe at risk from Chinese tech, says security think tank
raw_text:
European telecoms and computer infrastructure is vulnerable to hostile state interference with Chinese equipment suppliers such as Huawei and ZTE deeply embedded in parts of Europe’s networks, a research report claims.

The study by defence and security think tank Rusi warns that Europe’s patchwork approach to assessing risks from equipment suppliers means the security of critical national infrastructure is at risk from espionage and cyber attacks.

The report comes after a warning from MI5 that China’s Ministry of State Security is using a front company to fund research at UK universities, allowing it to gain access to technology that could pose a threat to the UK’s national security.

According to Rusi, the lack of agreement over what constitutes a high-risk ICT supplier has resulted in an inconsistent approach in Europe and the UK to Chinese suppliers, with many governments lacking basic information about what equipment is used in their networks.

This has led to widely different approaches by countries to using Chinese components in critical infrastructure, with Chinese suppliers accounting for nearly 60% of Germany’s 5G radio access network, compared with 30% in Spain and only 20% in the UK.

Spain, for example, awarded Chinese telecoms company Huawei a €12m contract for its OceanStor cloud storage servers, which were used to store recordings of judicial wiretaps.

The deal alarmed US lawmakers, who last year raised concerns that the Chinese government could gain access to highly sensitive data, including the ability to monitor Spanish investigations into Chinese spies.

Security risks posed by China

China’s National Intelligence and Counter-Espionage laws require private companies to supply data to the state on request.

There is deep coordination between Chinese businesses and the state, with Chinese firms legally required to host representatives of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) on their premises.

China also compels companies operating in the country to report software flaws to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology within 48 hours of their discovery, while prohibiting their disclosure outside of the country.

This gives China’s intelligence services early and privileged access to vulnerabilities that can be exploited by the state to hack into western companies and governments.

Source: Rusi

Security vulnerabilities

National security legislation in China enables Chinese authorities to control technology suppliers, such as telecoms supplier Huawei. It also provides a mechanism for the Chinese government to harvest security vulnerabilities that could be used to launch hacking attacks (see box: Security risks posed by China). There are also concerns that Chinese companies could withhold updates or maintenance for key services during political crises or conflict.

The report urges the UK to introduce legislation to protect the wider critical national infrastructure beyond telecoms and public sector procurement to give government powers to restrict the use of technology that could pose a risk more widely.

The UK has blocked Huawei from the 5G network and Chinese video camera suppliers from use by government departments, but has so far not intervened to assess and remove high-risk suppliers from other parts of the critical national infrastructure.

An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, if passed, will give the government powers to ban technology suppliers on national security grounds, without having to publicly designate the supplier as a national security risk.

Across Europe, the report identifies a gap between legislative ambition to restrict components that may cause a security risk and the implementation of measures to limit the deployment of Chinese technology in critical applications.

“Closing that gap will require not only stronger laws but also deeper institutional capacity, greater economic courage and a willingness to treat technology procurement as an instrument of strategic policy rather than a compliance exercise,” the report states.

MI5 warning to universities

Rusi’s report follows a warning by MI5 that more than 100 UK-linked academics have received funding from a research institute with strong ties to China’s Ministry of State Security.

UK academics have contributed to projects funded by the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) on artificial intelligence, cyber security, covert communications systems and steganography, which actively support Chinese espionage.

Academics could be subject to criminal consequences under the National Security Act 2023 if they knowingly materially assisted a foreign intelligence service, or ought reasonably to have known they were doing so, according to the MI5 advisory. 

How Europe and the UK have managed the risks of overseas suppliers

2005: British Telecom gives Huawei its first major contract in the UK.

2019: Political concerns are raised about existence of backdoors that would allow Huawei to access data.

2020: The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre found that none of the vulnerabilities in Huawei equipment were the result of state control or influence.

2020: Sweden excludes Huawei and ZTE from 5G networks on national security grounds.

July 2020: UK announces plans, which became legally binding, to strip Huawei equipment from the 5G network by December 2027 following US pressure.

2020: EU introduces a voluntary ‘Toolbox for 5G Security’ giving guidelines for managing high-risk telecoms suppliers.

2021: Germany passes the IT Security law 2.0, which allows the Ministry of Interior to exclude components from critical national infrastructure.

2021: The UK introduces the National Security and Investment Act, giving the UK power to screen and block foreign investments from Chinese. companies.

2021: UK introduces the Telecommunications Security Act, which gives government powers to designate equipment suppliers as high risk.

March 2022: Germany warns against the use of Kaspersky anti-virus software following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

November 2022: UK instructs government departments to remove cameras and surveillance systems supplied by Chinese suppliers.

2023: The European Commission explicitly states that Huawei and ZTE represent materially higher risks than other 5G suppliers.

2023: UK introduces the Procurement Act, which allows suppliers to the public sector to be excluded for national security reasons.

July 2024: Germany opts to phase out Chinese suppliers from ‘core’ 5G network.

2025: A report by Reuters raises concerns about the security risks of Chinese solar panel inverters.

2025: Germany announces it will not allow components from China in its 6G network.

2025: Germany implements the EU NIS2 Directive, which expands the scope of cyber security requirements to cover critical national infrastructure operators and large companies. It allows the German government to limit the use of critical components seen to pose a security risk.

2026: A review by the US Department of Energy found no evidence of backdoors in Chinese solar power inverters.

January 2026: The European Commission proposes amendments to the EU Cyber Security Act that, if enacted, will give the Commission powers to exclude high-risk suppliers, such as Huawei and ZTE, from critical sectors.

March 2026: UK government blocks a Chinese wind turbine manufacturer from building a factory in Scotland on national security grounds.

Source: Rusi

title: NRF Europe: tech transformations prevalent among major retailers
raw_text:
Retail executives from leading merchants and specialist technology providers returned to Paris for the second European event from the US-based National Retail Federation (NRF) that showcases cutting-edge technologies and provides a platform for the latest industry thinking.

Not surprisingly at such events, artificial intelligence (AI) is inescapable, but what was also evident this year at NRF Europe was the growing body of evidence that larger organisations are integrating AI-powered solutions alongside undertaking wholesale changes to their underlying technology infrastructures.

This has certainly been the case at Debenhams, which offloaded its physical stores and has adopted an online marketplace model selling products from 25,000 different brands and retailers, which does not involve holding any products in warehouses.

Dan Finley, CEO of Debenhams, says: “It’s been a fundamental transformation of the business model and it’s worked really well. We now see ourselves as a tech-led business. We’ve completely changed all the technology over the lpst two years. It’s delivered greater efficiencies.”

On top of the core IT systems, AI is being used to revolutionise areas such as the merchandising function, with price changes now possible across the 25,000-30,000 brands’ products in only minutes, and website content including descriptions and images can be created using these tools rather than involving a whole team of people.

Debenhams has also put a virtual assistant into the hands of all its customers that enables them to navigate through the company’s now massive inventory and focus in on exactly what they are after. “We are seeing much more expansive search terms and questions being asked. As agentic commerce company’s monetise their services [through advertising], then it will be an evolution for customers,” says Finley.

Home décor and furniture retailer Westwing has also undergone a fundamental technology overhaul. Andreas Hoerning, CEO of Westwing Group, says: “We shifted from our own tech stack to Shopify … moving from our own stack to a software-as-a-service [SaaS] model was a tough decision. As this model has evolved, there have been more off-the-shelf solutions available – whereas 15 years ago, you had to build things yourself. While the front end is still handled in-house all the other technology [for the back end] is SaaS, which simplifies things and enables us to stay ahead with our technology.”

This change has helped it shift its business model away from selling third-party brands to being a retailer of mainly own-label goods. He says 65% of its sales are now generated from in-house designed own-label products (accounting for 90% of margins) across around 5,000 lines compared with the previous 100% of goods from third-party brands, with their lesser margins.

A similar journey is being undertaken by Polish-based Zabka Group that has both repositioned itself as a more modern, dynamic convenience store – attracting a younger audience to its ready meals and hot food-to-go ranges – and a transformation of its technology that has driven great efficiencies and given it the flexibility to build capabilities such as a “super app”.

Tomasz Blicharski, incoming CEO of Zabka Group, says this move has helped it attract top technology talent who have constructed a solution for running the business much more efficiently. At the heart of this is the creation of data lakes, on top of which services have been built such as pricing, assortment and transportation.

“We’ve moved to higher margin products and differentiated formats with different ranges. Every single store now has its own unique planogram that’s created automatically based on the data,” he says, adding that differentiated pricing is also used across its stores that now number 13,000 in Poland and 300 in Romania.

The swing towards electronic pricing labels 

Pricing has certainly risen up the agenda of retailers and the power to be able to use data to determine prices more intelligently and change them swiftly is now regarded as extremely attractive. Hence all the major grocery chains around the world are rolling out Electronic Shelf-edge Labels (ESLs) along with the back-end pricing intelligence tools to better use price as a lever to improve efficiency and boost margins.

Like other businesses, Morrisons has found ESLs can play an increasingly important role beyond simply changing prices quickly. Gordon Macpherson, group productivity director at Morrisons, says: “The original premise was to save time, because we have 5,000-6,000 prices changes made on an evening … but as we continue to see online sales grow, then we will see how we can use the tech for quick-commerce. We get the benefits when all the tech interplays in-store.”

What attracted attention at NRF Europe was its use of the labels for “pick-by-light” that has been piloted to help colleagues navigate around its stores when picking for online orders. They are assigned one of seven colours and the label flashes this colour on the relevant product that they need to pick next for the order or the quick-commerce deliveries they are fulfilling.

The pilot has increased pick rate efficiency by 10% – with improvements in both speed and accuracy – that has given Morrisons the confidence to roll it out and give customers the capability to find products on the shelf via the flashing labels. Macpherson has noted the success by Walmart in the US, and so Morrisons will soon be enabling shoppers to select a product within the supermarket’s app and for this to prompt the label to flash.

Within the Innovators Showcase area of NRF Europe, AI solutions were certainly prevalent and in various instances sought to bring together disparate data sources and inject large language model (LLM) and machine learning capabilities to bring insights and intelligence into retailers’ businesses. Fashion was a category of particular attention as it is notable for its fragmented data sources and workflows.. 

Aristo AI brings together data sourced from across a business – including from the brand DNA documents through to design drawings and photo-shoots – and integrating this with a company’s Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) system before feeding it into a single unified system.

It is a similar story at Maeve AI, which also has a solution that plugs into a PLM as well as sourcing data from a fashion retailer’s sales and returns systems and then uses LLMs to identify errors in product designs before they move into the production process. These errors can include quality issues on certain materials, higher returns from specific suppliers and size issues with certain components.

Phoebe Gormley, founder of Maeve AI, says: “If you make a bad decision and then make products with it, then you have a problem. Once it’s baked into a product, then it’s the e-commerce teams who will have to deal with it and discount the products. These micro decisions can make a big difference.”

Retail executives from leading merchants and specialist technology providers returned to Paris for the second European event from the US-based National Retail Federation (NRF) that showcases cutting-edge technologies and provides a platform for the latest industry thinking.

Not surprisingly at such events, artificial intelligence (AI) is inescapable, but what was also evident this year at NRF Europe was the growing body of evidence that larger organisations are integrating AI-powered solutions alongside undertaking wholesale changes to their underlying technology infrastructures.

This has certainly been the case at Debenhams, which offloaded its physical stores and has adopted an online marketplace model selling products from 25,000 different brands and retailers, which does not involve holding any products in warehouses.

Dan Finley, CEO of Debenhams, says: “It’s been a fundamental transformation of the business model and it’s worked really well. We now see ourselves as a tech-led business. We’ve completely changed all the technology over the lpst two years. It’s delivered greater efficiencies.”

On top of the core IT systems, AI is being used to revolutionise areas such as the merchandising function, with price changes now possible across the 25,000-30,000 brands’ products in only minutes, and website content including descriptions and images can be created using these tools rather than involving a whole team of people.

Debenhams has also put a virtual assistant into the hands of all its customers that enables them to navigate through the company’s now massive inventory and focus in on exactly what they are after.

title: UK data regulator restructures amid allegations of ‘toxic’ workplace culture
raw_text:
The UK’s data regulator has rebranded and restructured, but critics question the lack of data protection expertise at the top of the organisation, while lingering concerns about a “toxic workplace culture” stemming from the organisation’s leadership persist among staff.

On 30 September 2026, the UK Information Commission took over the functions of the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), transferring the statutory powers and responsibilities previously vested in the Information Commissioner role to a board that will instead take collective responsibility for regulatory decisions.

The transition follows the resignation of the previous head, John Edwards, in June 2026, who left after an independent workplace investigation upheld multiple allegations of harassment and bullying against him.

Multiple ICO sources previously told Computer Weekly in July 2026 that the regulator’s internal problems were not limited to Edwards alone, and extended to the wider leadership team, who were aware of his conduct but failed to take action to protect staff.

They specifically accused the regulator’s senior leadership – many of whom are being carried over to the new Information Commission – of upholding a toxic workplace culture that ultimately made it a “less effective” regulator.

Staff response

Disaffected staff, organising with the Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS), have responded to the regulator’s rebrand and restructure by holding a “day of activity” to demand accountability for the leadership’s failures.

“The opening of a new headquarters and a rebrand cannot be allowed to distract from the serious concerns staff have raised about the culture within the organisation,” said PCS general secretary Fran Heathcote. “Our members want to see real accountability, a fully independent investigation and meaningful action to ensure that everyone can work in an environment free from bullying, harassment and discrimination.”

The action – which includes calling for a genuinely independent investigation into the leadership and workplace culture, and leafleting visitors and staff at the new headquarters – coincides with the opening of the regulator’s new Manchester headquarters, and the appointment of a new board.

The PCS said there is growing dissatisfaction and a declining sense of pride in working at the ICO among staff, who are unhappy with the continued lack of accountability for senior leadership and conduct that has “contributed to a climate of fear” at the organisation.

It added that a new name and headquarters will not, on their own, address the serious issues impacting staff well-being and safety.

According to a recent internal staff survey conducted by the ICO in the wake of Edwards’ departure, almost one in four employees had experienced or witnessed bullying, harassment or discrimination in the previous 12 months, with more than a third of those incidents allegedly involving senior staff.

As a result, just 34% of employees said they felt safe speaking up or challenging the way things are done at the organisation.

This marks an increase from a previous internal survey conducted in October 2025, which found that 10% of ICO staff experienced or witnessed bullying and harassment, with women twice as likely to experience that as men.

Privacy and data protection professionals outside of the ICO have also expressed concern about the internal culture and leadership of the rebranded regulator.

A source close to the Information Commission told Computer Weekly that the regulator had an opportunity to reset, but that it would require new leadership.

“John Edwards’ issues have really damaged the standing and the reputation of the office,” he said. “They have got the new non-execs. They are going to have a new chair and a new permanent chief executive, so there is an opportunity for them.”

But the source said the Information Commission needed to bring in a new chief executive to work alongside Edwards’ replacement if the reset was to be seen as credible.

“If you just have a coronation and just say, ‘well, you have been there forever so you can just have the permanent role’, it’s not going to be seen as a step to change the culture,” he added.

The Information Commissioner’s Office has entered into 16 non-disclosure agreements with current or former employees at a cost of £354,000 since January 2022. Nine of the agreements included clauses to prevent former employees making disparaging comments about their former employer, according to a Freedom of Information disclosure published today.

Another privacy professional who asked not to be named said allegations of a toxic workforce were a “monumental shambles” and a distraction for the organisation.

“It’s a big blow to the ICO at a time when it should and cold be doing some meaningful things on privacy, safety and the impact of emerging tech,” they said.

An ‘independent’ review?

While technology secretary Liz Kendall announced on 8 July that the government will be launching an “independent review into the culture, accountability and governance of the ICO”, this is yet to begin.

The ICO also confirmed at the time that it will be involved in the “independent review” of its workplace culture and practices.

While the union sent a letter to digital secretary Lisa Nandy – who has responsibility for oversight of the commission since the government’s abolition of the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) – raising concerns about the safety of ICO workers and asking to set a meeting, it says it is yet to receive a response after nearly two months.

The PCS has expressed concern about the lack of clear assurances over whether any investigation will have the scope and authority needed to hold those responsible accountable.

Lawrence Dunne, PCS industrial officer for the ICO, told Computer Weekly that any independent review will need to avoid the perception that the previous leadership has influence over the process, and must be “practically separate from the leadership”, as a significant part of the workforce have no confidence in their ability to deal with the issues themselves.

“It’s a matter of accountability,” he said. “Ultimately before ICO can move on its workforce, and the public, frankly, they deserve answers about how it got to that stage – it was not, and it was never the case, of one bad apple.

“The allegations around Edwards and the incidents that were allowed to happen took place because of an environment that fostered this sort of behaviour unfortunately.”

He also expressed “disappointment” that, despite writing to Nandy two months ago, DCMS is still yet to respond, or set a meeting with the workers or their union.

Dunne concluded that an independent review is ultimately needed to establish exactly who in the senior leadership is responsible for what: “It’s not credible for them to launch a new era for the regulator – with a new building, board, name and revised powers – with the same leaders who have presided over an increasingly toxic workplace, without answers and accountability for how it got so bad.”

‘Zero-tolerance approach’

Computer Weekly contacted the Information Commission about every aspect of the story.

“Our recent internal survey results come at a time of significant change for the organisation as we transition to our new governance structure and when recent events have had an impact on our people and how they feel,” said a spokesperson.

“While the majority of colleagues continue to recommend the ICO as a great place to work, any reports of bullying and harassment are treated with the utmost seriousness and a zero-tolerance approach. We already have a number of actions in place to support our colleagues and we are working with them and our trade unions to listen, learn and take action.”

They added that, for the independent review, it is closely working with the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) to finalise the terms of reference and support it to progress, but the process is taking longer than expected due to the abolition of DSIT.

“Our leadership share our colleagues’ desire for this to proceed at pace and we will continue to keep staff updated,” they said.

“We take seriously our responsibility to balance both privacy and transparency in every aspect of our work. As is standard in many workplaces, we have previously agreed a small number of confidential settlements as an appropriate way to resolve employment disputes. While we do not comment on individual settlements, each is considered on its own circumstances.”

Responding to Computer Weekly’s questions, a DCMS spokesperson said: “The government is committed to ensuring the Information Commission has strong governance, accountability and leadership, and that the concerns raised about its workplace culture are properly examined through an independent process. We are progressing plans for the review and will provide further details in due course.”

Neither the commission nor DCMS commented on whether Paul Arnold will need to be replaced if the regulator’s reset is to be seen as credible.

A change of structure

The structure of the ICO will bring it in line with other regulators, with responsibility for making decisions now being vested in a board, rather than an individual commissioner.

The Information Commission appointed seven non-executive members in July 2026, who will play a role in the organisation’s governance strategy from today.

However, the structure leaves a lack of data protection expertise at the top of the organisation, with none of the non-executives having data protection expertise.

“Decision-making is going to fall quite a few layers from the top,” said the source close to the ICO. “And there is a degree of uncertainty because at least with a commissioner, you know where the commissioner stands.”

DCMS is recruiting for a permanent chair of the Information Commission, with a decision expected by Spring 2027.

Maggie Carver, former deputy chair of Ofcom and a company director, has been appointed deputy chair of the Information Commission.

  • UK data watchdog accused of dragging feet on eVisa investigation: Despite longstanding data protection issues with the Home Office’s electronic visa system being flagged five months ago, the UK’s data regulator is yet to take any action.
  • ICO fines Cl0p victim South Staffs Water over data breach: The ICO has levied a reduced fine on South Staffordshire Water following cyber improvements in the wake of a Cl0p ransomware attack.

The new governance model for the Information Commission was established in the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, which received royal assent in June 2025.

The act gave the ICO powers to compel witnesses, who may be current or former employees of an organisation under investigation to attend an interview and answer questions, and to require organisations to disclose documents relevant to an investigation.

It also gained powers to introduce higher fines to organisations involved in nuisance emails, text messages and calls, raising the cap from a maximum of £500,0000 to £17.5m, or 4% of annual turnover.

James Moss, director of Cyber Investigations at law firm Addleshaw Goddard, told Computer Weekly that the change in structure was an opportunity, but it was the people, rather than the structure that would make a difference.

“The commission will need a strong and able chair and a strong and able permanent chief exec working alongside a senior leadership team who can effectively prioritise the work the Information Commission has in front of it, decide what they want to achieve and set about working to achieve it,” he said. “Without those things, the change of structure risks being a missed opportunity.”

Lee Ramsay, managing knowledge lawyer at law firm Lewis Silkin, told Computer Weekly that having an executive board with multidisciplinary experience would bring the Information Commission in line with other regulators.

“You don’t need to have data protection specialists to be effective,” she said. “A board is really there to set strategy, provide the oversight and challenge, and then your deep technical expertise is sitting within the organisation.”

Joe Jones, director of research and insights at the IAPP, a professional association for privacy professionals, said the restructuring was an overdue move.

“With a new board and recruitment underway to identify a chair, we don’t yet know whether the governance model, designed to distribute power and responsibility to a board, will form a clear identity and approach from the ICO, in the way that many past commissioners have defined and steered the ICO’s approach,” he said.

Jones said the changes might result in greater consistency when leadership at the Information Commission changes, with longer-term priorities, instantiations and enforcement that “aren’t at the mercy of changes in commissioners”.

title: Government faces judicial review over Post Office Capture redress
raw_text:
The husband of a former subpostmaster, who had her financial and mental health destroyed at the hands of the Post Office, is preparing a judicial review to challenge the government’s financial redress decisions.

In another twist in the Post Office Horizon scandal, Ken Tooby has warned the government that he will apply for judicial review of the decision to award him less than a third of a claim submitted on behalf of his late wife, June Tooby, who was blamed for losses recorded on the organisation’s faulty Capture software.

A judicial review would see a judge evaluate the lawfulness of decisions over the value of the offer and Tooby’s rejected appeal against it. This could impact a small cohort of former subpostmasters who suffered life-changing losses through Capture but have received derisory redress offers.

A government spokesperson said: “After more than two decades fighting for justice, subpostmasters and their families are finally receiving recognition and redress from the impacts of the Capture software.

“To date, over £8.7 million has been awarded to people affected by the [Capture] scandal, with offers set by an independent panel. We are working tirelessly to make sure every victim gets the justice and compensation they deserve as soon as possible. We do not comment on individual cases, and it would be inappropriate for the Department to comment on the potential legal action.”

June Tooby, who died in 2020, was a subpostmaster in County Durham. Her contract was terminated after nearly two decades when she had unexplained shortfalls. She had used Capture at the branch for almost a decade.

In 2024, an independent investigation was commissioned into Capture, which found there was a “reasonable likelihood” it had caused shortfalls in branch accounts, which ruined lives.

Tooby was the first former Capture user to receive an official apology from the Post Office for her treatment. In a letter, the Post Office wrote to Ken Tooby: “It is clear through the efforts of former postmasters and their families that there were significant failings at Post Office relating to Capture. We are truly sorry for these failings and their impact on all concerned, including your late wife, June.”

Capture was a PC-based software application that pre-dated the Horizon system, which has been at the heart of the Post Office scandal.

Triggered by Horizon drama

Former subpostmasters, who used the system in the 1990s, came forward with their stories following ITV’s 2024 drama about the Post Office Horizon scandal.

It was the same month that Kevan Jones, an MP at the time who now sits in the House of Lords, highlighted evidence of injustices triggered by Capture losses.

This ignited a campaign and, by December, the government promised financial redress and justice for subpostmasters affected by Capture problems. This followed an independent investigation by forensic experts at Kroll, which found there was a “reasonable likelihood” the Post Office Capture software had caused accounting losses.

Capture was a different software to Horizon, but the way the Post Office dealt with unexplained losses was the same, with subpostmasters covering the shortfalls, which often put them in life-changing difficulties. Many went bankrupt and some were prosecuted and convicted for financial crimes.

In a 2018 group litigation, High Court Judge Peter Fraser ruled that the Post Office showed “oppressive behaviour” towards the subpostmasters who had experienced shortfalls.

Regarding the Post Office’s policy to force subpostmasters to cover unexplained losses, he wrote in his judgment: “There can be no excuse, in my judgment, for an entity such as the Post Office to mis-state, in such clearly expressed terms, in letters that threaten legal action, the extent of the contractual obligation upon a [subpostmaster] for losses.

“The only reason for doing so, in my judgment, must have been to lead the recipients to believe that they had absolutely no option but to pay the sums demanded. It is oppressive behaviour.”

Diffrent treatment

After the huge court victory, the Post Office was forced to set up schemes to compensate effected subpostmasters. But former Capture users were not permitted to join Horizon shortfall redress schemes to make claims related to Capture, but were offered the chance to claim through a separate Capture redress scheme.

The Capture redress scheme is offering initial payments of £10,000 – with final award bands up to £300,000 – to subpostmasters who suffered because of the software’s flaws, with “exceptional cases” receiving payments above the upper limit.

At the time, a former subpostmaster who suffered at the hands of the Post Office’s faulty software said the announced compensation scheme “discriminates” against claimants.

Ken Tooby has been offered less than half of the amount claim. Offers to other Capture users, classed as exceptional cases, fall well below claims.

As reported previously by Computer Weekly, former subpostmaster Lee Bowerman, who is one of four “exceptional cases”, received a financial settlement offer through the Capture redress scheme which equated to just 7% of his professionally calculated claim.

The former subpostmaster in South Wales, who lost his business more than 30 years ago, was part of a group that helped the government department design the scheme.

Bowerman complained that consequential losses were not included in the offer and that there was limited opportunity to appeal decisions on redress awards. He called for parity with former Horizon users who were also affected in the Post Office scandal.

In the letter sent to former Department for Business and Trade (DBT) minister Blair McDougall MP, Bowerman wrote: “Throughout every meeting, without exception, we were explicitly assured that there would be full parity with the Horizon redress schemes. These assurances were clear and repeated.”

Bowerman said this has not happened in his case.

Solicitor Neil Hudgell of Hudgell Solicitors, which represents many former Capture users, said the Capture redress scheme “was designed to be light touch to avoid the long, torturous process of many of the other schemes”.

Hudgell  added: “In the main part, it has been able to deliver speedier redress to the majority of Claimants, that’s some good news. However, for the most seriously affected, it falls badly short in our view in achieving fairness consistent with other victims of the scandal.

“Government are aware of our concerns and we continue in dialogue with them in the hope of avoiding costly and time-consuming legal proceedings. Victims that have endured the scandal for upwards of 30 years need closure but equally need that to be on terms that are fair and reflect the losses that they have endured during that time.”

title: Has the time arrived for the retail chief AI officer?
raw_text:
Back in February 2018, Computer Weekly asked the question, “What are the retail jobs that don’t exist yet?”.

In the midst of rapid technological change impacting the industry, it was a future-gazing piece speculating what roles retailers might soon be looking for considering the ongoing digital evolution, advancement in tech sophistication and changing customer demands.

Then Missguided chief technology officer (CTO) John Allen was quoted predicting how automation and artificial intelligence (AI) best practice in retail will result in machines applying general processing rules, but with people on hand to intervene to make more specific commercial decisions when needed. That vision has become a reality retail is now embracing.

But instead of the mooted AI intervention officer job role, we’re seeing fully fledged chief AI officers (CAIOs) enter the fray.

Mohsen Ghasempour, an experienced technology leader with a PHD in computer science and CAIO at B&Q parent company Kingfisher Group, was announced as Morrisons’ first CAIO in September. Ghasempour remains very much in the minority as someone in retail with that job title – although US retail chain Target appointed Chandhu Nair as its first CAIO in August, and there is a groundswell of support and potential commercial necessity for others to join him.

In his newly created role at Morrisons, Ghasempour is tasked with establishing a central data science and AI function for Morrisons that will take overall responsibility for data and AI strategy. In a varied job spec, the focus of the function at the grocer will be on customer growth, empowering colleagues, operational efficiency, and manufacturing and commercial excellence.

He reports directly to the CEO, Rami Baitiéh, who is a vocal advocate of finding ways to use AI to drive business success.

The line of reporting to the top shows how seriously the supermarket chain is taking the AI era. Baitiéh said the appointment reflects Morrisons’ commitment to “embracing the opportunities in data and AI at pace, with focus and in the right way”.

Ghasempour himself spoke of helping the business “make effective and responsible use of AI in the years ahead” that, he hopes, will deliver real benefits for customers and colleagues alike.

Responsible AI

The use of the adjective “responsible” by Morrisons’ new recruit is pertinent against the current political and economic backdrop.

US president Donald Trump met with tech company leaders at the end of September to agree voluntary AI safety standards. LinkedIn research released the same week shows the number of AI safety-related roles listed on its pages had grown by 91% over the previous year.

Meanwhile, the Australian government set up a taskforce in September to review how it responds to AI-related cyber incidents, after it emerged an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a Medicare website run by Services Australia.

On 29 September, Computer Weekly caught up with a retailer with “responsible AI” in his job title. The meeting place was the Mach Alliance’s Mach X event in Amsterdam, which ran for two days and brought together retailers and other merchants with a raft of tech companies promising to bring composable, connected and open tech products to market.

Just two years ago, few retailers would have had a senior executive with “responsible AI” in their job title. Today, as AI moves from experimentation into the heart of retail operations, roles such as that held by Pratyush Sinha are beginning to emerge.

Sinha, who has just left his position as senior director and head of responsible AI at sports equipment retailer Decathlon, told this publication traditional technology leaders have historically been concerned with infrastructure, systems, deployment and cost. But autonomous AI systems are increasingly having a direct influence on organisational outcomes.

“Agentic systems are in equal parts competing with infrastructure,” says Sinha. “The role of CIO was to get the most stable, confident and cost-efficient infrastructure in place that serves the company’s outcomes. Now agentic systems are doing much of this.”

His conclusion is that the traditional technology hierarchy may itself need to change.

“The CAIO role is more relevant in some organisations now than having a CIO or CTO or chief data officer,” says Sinha.

  • Some 90% of retailers planning to boost spending on artificial intelligence to optimise e-commerce operations, as new research identifies different AI shopper personas and The Delivery Conference provides forum for debate.
  • Ann Summers’ technology and supply chain director Jeannette Copeland talks through lessons learned during the retailer’s recent ESB overhaul.

Sinha, who followed Barbara Martin Coppola from Ikea to Decathlon in 2022 when she moved from chief digital officer at the furniture retailer to take on the CEO role at the sports chain, said he has long considered “algorithmic accountability” in his work.

The principle is relatively straightforward, he notes, saying if an algorithm is going to be deployed in a product, a retailer needs to understand how reliably it works and what happens when it encounters the messy complexity of the real world.

“For me, what it means is that everything is observed, everything is re-constructible and everything is explainable,” he says of the key aspects of his role as head of responsible AI.

With increasingly sophisticated AI models, particularly large language models, understanding exactly why a system produces a particular answer can be extremely difficult. For Sinha, the answer is not to treat responsible AI as a separate ethical exercise bolted onto technology projects – it needs to become part of how products are designed, trained and evaluated.

One major area of focus for Sinha at Decathlon was to build an AI-powered e-commerce search function, and he notes this is where there is a huge responsibility to avoid bias in the search function’s results. One role of the head of responsible AI is to identify the difference between harmful bias and relevant context, he explains.

“Let’s say a brown man, like me, [inserts into a search or chat function] that ‘I’m a brown man and I need shoes’ and the search finds shoes that are brown in colour – that will be harmful bias,” he notes.

“But if a pregnant woman comes and says, ‘I’m pregnant and I need shoes’ and the model ignores the fact that there is pregnancy, that will be missing the context. So, knowing the difference between harmful bias and useful context is responsible AI.”

Sinha says search systems need to be designed so they recognise these important factors in order not to upset customers or divert consumers to rival retailers.

Changing responsibilities

Sinha predicts that another emerging role in retail tech and wider business could be the “multi-agent architect”.

The reason is because AI systems are now capable of doing more than simply responding to prompts or retrieving information.

“Now AI can reason,” he says. “Now AI can exercise judgement. And now AI can look around the corner.”

Agentic systems can, in his description, reason, make judgements and act – potentially coordinating several AI agents to achieve a particular business outcome. And architects will be – and already are, in his view – needed to orchestrate all of that in the form of a specific job role.

Currently, he argues, the responsibilities for this new function sit somewhat “under the radar”, spread across existing technology jobs. As agentic systems become more deeply embedded in businesses, however, he expects the need for dedicated responsibility to become clearer.

Indeed, roles and responsibilities of the tech, engineering and security teams was a hot topic throughout the Mach X event.

Debating whose role is it to articulate any security consequences of AI deployment and what the rules are regarding AI usage, Simon Edwards, cyber security architect at shirtmaker and formalwear retailer Charles Tyrwhitt, called it a “shared responsibility”.

“It’s never us as a single function,” he explained. “This is a new skill the business needs to adopt and a new responsibility it needs to adopt.”

Neil Bennett, chief information security officer at the Post Office, who joined Edwards in a panel debate on the subject, added: “It’s a combination – it’s partly us, its partly legal, it’s partly DP [data protection], it’s a combination of different people who have a stake in this and a combination of people who have a detailed understanding.”

Blending old and new

Another common theme discussed in Amsterdam was the importance of finding the right blend between the new and the old guard.

Fresh young talent leaving university, already tooled up with AI usage knowledge and bursting with ideas on how to implement it into the businesses they are joining, is now mixing with long-term IT practitioners who have grown up with the importance of risk management, guardrails and pragmatism when it comes to tech deployment.

There’s room for both types in the industry, according to panellists debating the new agentic ecosystem. 

Travis Hess, CEO at e-commerce platform provider Commerce (previously known as BigCommerce), said: “Thinking of human capital and what’s the most important attribute in the world of agentic – it’s curiosity.

“Those who are innately curious tend to do really well, but that also needs to be balanced with pragmatism.”

Andrew Clarson, digital marketing and commerce practice leader at Deloitte Digital, who chaired the discussion, added: “The level of experience people have now has been normalised because everything is brand new.

“The graduate coming out of university today is hungry and enthusiastic, and if they have the right personal attributes they can be just as – perhaps more – successful as someone with five years of actually increasingly irrelevant experience.”

Pace of change

The panel, which also featured Charles Tyrwhitt CTO Doug Wooten and MongoDB director of industry solutions Genevieve Broadhead, reflected on the risk to the retail industry of the pace of change in tech and the dangers of moving too fast with agentic commerce before relevant guardrails are implemented.

Wooten said he was confident the curious nature of the graduates coming into the industry will dovetail neatly with the more pragmatic characteristics typically associated with those who have worked in IT for many years. Each generation helps the other, he noted.

Broadhead suggested the new workforce generation coming through are not thinking about developing a skill and living with it for their whole career like their predecessors might have done.

“They are thinking, ‘I’ll use this for six months then I’ll learn something new, something new, something new’,” she added, noting a person’s ability to adapt and to change – and to not be scared of learning new things – will be a vital skill in the agentic age.

Back in February 2018, Computer Weekly asked the question, “What are the retail jobs that don’t exist yet?”.

In the midst of rapid technological change impacting the industry, it was a future-gazing piece speculating what roles retailers might soon be looking for considering the ongoing digital evolution, advancement in tech sophistication and changing customer demands.

Then Missguided chief technology officer (CTO) John Allen was quoted predicting how automation and artificial intelligence (AI) best practice in retail will result in machines applying general processing rules, but with people on hand to intervene to make more specific commercial decisions when needed. That vision has become a reality retail is now embracing.

But instead of the mooted AI intervention officer job role, we’re seeing fully fledged chief AI officers (CAIOs) enter the fray.

Mohsen Ghasempour, an experienced technology leader with a PHD in computer science and CAIO at B&Q parent company Kingfisher Group, was announced as Morrisons’ first CAIO in September. Ghasempour remains very much in the minority as someone in retail with that job title – although US retail chain Target appointed Chandhu Nair as its first CAIO in August, and there is a groundswell of support and potential commercial necessity for others to join him.

In his newly created role at Morrisons, Ghasempour is tasked with establishing a central data science and AI function for Morrisons that will take overall responsibility for data and AI strategy. In a varied job spec, the focus of the function at the grocer will be on customer growth, empowering colleagues, operational efficiency, and manufacturing and commercial excellence.

He reports directly to the CEO, Rami Baitiéh, who is a vocal advocate of finding ways to use AI to drive business success.

The line of reporting to the top shows how seriously the supermarket chain is taking the AI era.

title: CW@60: Making the next 60 years of British tech as glorious as the last
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

Britain is often portrayed - perhaps a little too masochistically at times - as having fallen irrevocably behind in the global technology race.

Certainly, when we look at the dominance of Silicon Valley and the growing technological power of China, there’s some uncomfortable truth in that. But what’s puzzling is Britain has repeatedly been very good at inventing the future. Long before the Apple and IBM personal computer revolution, British scientists and engineers were pioneering programmable computing.

The BBC Micro was particularly iconic. Developed by Acorn in conjunction with the BBC for its television series The Computer Programme, it was adopted widely by schools, granting a whole generation of British children their first experience of programming and computing.

The legacy went beyond that. Famously, out of UK firm Acorn’s work on RISC technology would ultimately emerge ARM, one of the most consequential British technology success stories. But even before that, Britain was leading the world. In the 1980s, Clive Sinclair’s ZX80 brought remarkably accessible computing into people’s homes, plugging straight into a television, while Alan Sugar’s Amstrad became another defining British technology success story.

A move to a ‘business is good’ mindset is overdue

The problem was what happens with all these amazing ideas. Britain can be great at innovation, but it is at best mediocre at taking those ideas to market, and genuinely poor at scaling them globally.

Time and again, six decades of British tech have shown us inventing something extraordinary and building a global technology company are two different skills. Maybe we’re better at producing eccentrics and maverick inventors than global CEOs - James Dyson is an example of an inventor who has built a globally recognised business around technology and Mike Lynch was a fantastic business creator. But both were exceptions to the rule.

Britain has no shortage of brilliant minds. Cambridge, my alma mater, is full of brilliant engineers, scientists and technologists, but where is the know-how to turn that intellectual TNT into globally scalable businesses?

Britain needs more entrepreneurs, greater confidence in entrepreneurship and a better understanding of how to commercialise technology.

That means changing the cultural narrative as well as the economic one. When an entrepreneur builds a successful company, it can employ thousands of people, create new capabilities and generate wealth that can be reinvested elsewhere. Britain needs to see that kind of success as something to celebrate and encourage, not something to apologise for.

The contrast with the US is revealing. I recently visited a US go-kart track run by teenage entrepreneurs who refurbished old karts and turned them into a business. I’d struggle to imagine many 19-year-olds in the UK doing the same.

Cultural differences

This cultural difference in appetite for risk and enterprise has serious implications for Britain’s future; not just in technology, but in creating the next generation of IP-rich businesses that generate revenues, tax and meaningful futures for founders and employees.

Britain once had role models in abundance. From Maurice Wilkes and Cambridge Consultants founders Tim Eiloart and David Southward, to Acorn’s Chris Curry and Hermann Hauser, Andy Hopper and Robin Saxby, and later David Chiswell, Raspberry Pi’s Eben Upton and Jack Lang - these are the people who helped build the Cambridge/Silicon Fen technology ecosystem and Britain’s wider technology story. Their names should be as recognisable to Gen Z as Bruno Mars and Tom Holland.

The lack of visible business and tech founder role models matters. It risks holding us back from making the next 60 years of British technology as potentially glorious as some of the last 60.

Genuine British IT world firsts, from Cambridge’s EDSAC and the Manchester Baby to Leo, the world’s first business computer, and the 1980s microcomputer revolution, show what happens when technological imagination and commercial execution align.

Britain has already demonstrated it can invent the future. The challenge is turning those inventions into global businesses. The ingredients remain - world-class universities, technical expertise and inventive entrepreneurs - but we need the confidence, commercial machinery and culture to turn those ingredients into many more global companies.

Dr John Bates is CEO of Doxis. He is part of the Cambridge University startup scene and a serial tech entrepreneur.

title: Members braced as Teachers’ Pension transfer approaches
raw_text:
Members of the UK’s Teachers’ Pension scheme are bracing themselves for the switchover to a new supplier at the start of next month, amid delays to pensions.

Indian IT giant Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) is set to take over the work from Capita after securing a 10-year Department for Education contract in 2023.

Capita has run the service for more than 20 years, but a blackout on the website is planned from 22 October to 2 November as the scheme is transferred to TCS.

MPs heard earlier last month that some teachers are experiencing problems.

In light of Capita’s disastrous takeover of the Civil Service Pension Scheme, a Westminster Hall debate was held, where MPs discussed the botched scheme.

During that packed-out meeting, Alison Bennet, Liberal Democrat MP for Mid Sussex, said she had been told teachers were experiencing problems with their pensions. She asked: “Are we seeing teachers go through the same ordeal [as civil servants]?

“I have received very concerning casework from teachers in my constituency who seem to be having similar or the same troubles with their pensions,” added Bennet. “The idea that the immense stress and potential financial hardship we’ve heard inflicted on civil servants has been [repeated] with teachers is appalling.”

Delays already

A Department for Education spokesperson said the scheme has some “clearly unacceptable” delays. “We understand that delays to bereavement payments can be distressing for families, and we expect Capita to work closely with those affected to resolve issues as quickly as possible and keep them informed throughout,” they said.

The government department confirmed the transfer will be complete on 1 November, with the website and member/employer portal available from 2 November. TCS and Capita were contacted for an update on progress, but the former declined to comment and the latter did not respond.

The Department for Education said bereavement cases are a priority area. It said it “recognises that delays can be distressing for those affected and have worked closely with Capita to monitor performance and drive improvements.  This includes reviewing IT contingency arrangements and securing additional resources to help limit delays. Progress continues to be monitored through the department’s contract management arrangements.”

The department is also working closely with TCS as part of the transition to the new administration contract.

Recent figures from the Department for Education show that during the period between 1 April 2026 and 30 June 2026, there were 2,103 bereavement cases involving a continuing entitlement processed by Capita as part of the Teachers’ Pension scheme administration contract. “An average of 89.06% of these cases were completed within the contractual target of seven working days,” it said. “The average completion time was just over eight working days.”

Precautionary advice

Teachers are being advised to make copies of data available as backup. One former teacher who is supporting teachers with concerns said there are thousands of anomalies in the data being transferred that could see teachers lose out. “I have been encouraging teachers to make copies of the data that they have available through the website,” he said. “Downloading their statements and copying their employment history into a spreadsheet.”

Comparing the transfer to the Civil Service Pension Scheme supplier switch, he said: “I would say that there are similarities but that we do not have the severity of hardship caused by teachers failing to be paid anything that appears to be the case with the civil service pensions for a large number. However, the issue with data husbandry is, and has been, ongoing.

“Unfortunately, I can see TCS might have similar problems once they get full access to all of the data given how many errors are flagged up at the last minute in the process when teachers apply for their pensions,” he added.

title: DWP insources Universal Credit checking work
raw_text:
The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is insourcing 2,700 staff from an outsourcing supplier and will now complete Universal Credit Review (UCR) work in-house.

Staff will transfer to the civil service from business services firm Teleperformance, which has run the service since 2024.

The government said the insourcing decision is not related to the supplier’s performance: “The decision was taken to deliver targeted case reviews internally for the next phase, as we work to deliver £17.3bn of savings by March 2031, and was not due to supplier performance. Both parties continue to work closely during this phase of transition from supplier to DWP. 

“This is part of wider plans targeting billions of pounds more in savings in the coming years by tackling fraud and error in the welfare system.” 

Disputed rationale

The Public and Commercial Services (PCS) Union said it has disputed the department’s rationale that UCR work should be outsourced since it became aware of the plans in 2023: “We argued that it would not deliver value for taxpayers’ money, that it would not deliver the work efficiently, and that this core civil service work should not be delivered for profit by the private sector.”

The PCS added: “Throughout the duration of the contract, frustrated members working for DWP on UCR have told PCS that it wasn’t working, that handovers from the private sector were not in good shape and created extra work for DWP staff.”

The union said that Teleperformance benefitted from a £368m contract signed in 2024.

As the government has announced plans for the “greatest wave of insourcing” in a generation, suppliers cannot afford to slip up. One civil service source said: “The political climate is highly relevant. Any [supplier] slip ups will build a clamour for a bigger and more aggressive insourcing programme.”

In March, Cabinet Office parliamentary secretary at the time Chris Ward said “the age of outsourcing will end” and announced plans to insource services.

“For decades, successive governments have been, at best, ambivalent about whether public services are delivered in-house,” he said. “At worst, we’ve had outsourcing by default, with public services hollowed out and sold off to the lowest bidder. That era ends today.”

Insourcing snowball

In April, the government terminated Capita’s Royal Mail pension scheme contract, citing failures to hit milestones.

The British Medical Association (BMA) recently called for the GP pension scheme to be brought in-house, claiming the current supplier Capita lacks the “ability” and “capacity” to run it.

The government is also in the process of planning a long-term strategy of bringing the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) in-house. The service administered by Capita has been a disaster since the supplier took over in December, with retired civil servants waiting months – nearly a year in some cases – for their pensions.

Disaster after disaster has prompted the government to make the decision, with a Cabinet Office spokesperson telling Computer Weekly that the government is “actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring this pension scheme back in-house”. 

Sally Jameson MP, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, said in a recent Westminster Hall debate: “We stood on a manifesto as a Labour government to have the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation. I am personally committed to that. I’ve said in this house before that I think that’s a priority for this [CSPS] scheme, but we can only do it when we make sure that it’s in the interest of the members. We’ve got to make sure that there is no disruption. We’ve got to do it in the smoothest and quickest way.”

In the same debate, Ian Byrne, MP for Liverpool West Derby, described the botched CSPS scheme as “the failure of outsourcing laid bare”.

The PCS union added: “The decision to insource [the DWP] work demonstrates again the failure of the private sector to deliver key public sector services.”

title: Five ways to make it to the tech C-suite
raw_text:
If you’ve made it to a management or director role in technology, you may well have aspirations to make it to the tech C-suite as a CIO, CTO or other leadership position. But competition amongst talented professionals is fierce, while the advent of AI means that the technology landscape is changing and moving at a pace never seen before.

 So, how can you maximise your chances of making it to the tech C-suite? Here are five key tips from our experience of supporting organisations in their executive leadership searches.

1. Prove yourself through results – and be prepared to wait. To really stand a chance of making the C-suite, you’ll need a deep and broad track record of leading impactful projects, driving change and transformation underpinned by innovative tech-based solutions. What boards are most interested in is results: outcomes rather than job titles. Make sure you can show what you’ve actually achieved, how you did that, and the financial and or performance/productivity impact it had for the organisation. Don’t expect your C-suite ambition to happen straightaway. Following on from working in junior and management roles, generally a candidate would spend 5-10 years operating at Director level, perhaps reporting to a CIO. Be realistic about your strengths and weaknesses, and any gaps in your experience you need to fill. For example, a strong track record on the engineering, systems and apps side – the front-office, customer-facing applications of tech – is generally at a premium. So if your experience lies more in the back-office infrastructure and networking domain, look for opportunities to build your credentials in frontline digital, data and AI where technology translates into measurable business outcomes.

2. Be flexible about career paths. If you’re working in a FTSE or other business, there is the question of whether you want to stay in that environment all of your career – or whether you would be open to moving to an SME or start-up as CIO or other tech leadership role as a first step (before potentially going back to a FTSE again). Conversely, if you’re in an SME or start-up now, do you want to try to get into a bigger corporate and work your way up in an environment where there may be more potential routes up? That’s a pathway we quite often see – the CTO of a start-up moving into a Director role in a large corporate, for example. But there are challenges involved both ways due to the significant differences in working environment, team sizes and culture. A FTSE hiring manager may be concerned that someone from a start-up will struggle to adapt to the more formal and process-driven environment in their business, while leaders in a start-up may worry that a candidate moving from a corporate may not fit the agile culture. You really need to think hard about whether such a switch would work for you: do you have the ability to adapt?

 3. Upskill yourself and gain experience in AI. The rise of AI has fundamentally altered conversations around executive hiring as our wider client base seek leaders who understand how AI can be applied responsibly and effectively at an enterprise level. The pace of change has been extraordinary. AI now features in some way in almost every senior hiring mandate we receive: knowledge and experience of AI, along with wider digital and data literacy, are becoming the expected currency of tech leadership. Our clients, without exception, are telling us that their new technology leaders need to be able to straddle the old and the new, embracing AI in a meaningful and benefits aligned manner. Tech leaders need to be skilled in developing practical AI strategies aligned to organisational goals and driving adoption across the workforce. Put your hand up for any AI project opportunities in your current role. This isn’t just about technical understanding either – balancing innovation with governance, ethics, security and risk management is also critical, so look for opportunities to contribute to these key aspects.

 4. Focus on personal development and leadership skills. Being a tech leader these days is about much more than just being a technology expert. Boards are looking for rounded leaders: people who understand the commercial drivers, are critical thinkers, excellent communicators, embrace innovation, can deal with ambiguity, and have the ability to lead, manage and inspire teams. Work on your soft skills. If there is training available here, take it. Tech leaders need high emotional intelligence and be able to manage diverse teams. Learn from others you admire – is there an opportunity to get a mentor? A common theme amongst many successful tech leaders is that they have proactively sought out mentors to support them with their personal development, helping them reflect and learn about everything from business and strategic thinking to personal resilience and leadership skills.

5. Develop your personal brand. This is an area that some tech leaders pay significant attention to. Building your profile in the market obviously helps you get noticed and may open up doors. Look for opportunities to get involved in PR and marketing activities, such as contributing to articles, speaking at events and participating in webinars, panels and podcasts.  Consider also getting involved with activities that resonate with you personally, such as supporting efforts to increase diversity in tech or open up pathways into the profession. All of these activities help you build your network, be more visible and uncover opportunities.

 They say Rome wasn’t built in a day – and neither are tech leadership careers. Have patience. Build a clear plan, invest in your technical skills and work on your leadership capabilities. In that way, you’ll be better equipped to take advantage of the opportunities that arise along the way.
