title: Teen hacker arrested amid KillSec cyber gang takedown
raw_text:
Authorities in Spain have arrested a 16-year-old boy accused of involvement in the KillSec ransomware gang, which is thought to have conducted over 1,000 cyber attacks over the past couple of years.

The unnamed minor, who is a Romanian national, was taken into custody in a joint operation by Spain’s national Guardia Civil police force and the Catalan authorities, following searches at two addresses in the southern city of Alicante, one a private home, the other a hotel.

The Guardia Civil said its officers seized computer equipment, mobile phones, cryptocurrency wallets, and various tools designed to mask the gang’s activities.

The arrest comes amid a wider takedown operation – coordinated by Hamburg state authorities in Germany – targeting the KillSec ransomware gang. Dubbed Operation KillSwitch, the sting saw searches conducted in Greece, Romania and the UK, and two additional arrests made. Law enforcement also seized KillSec’s leak site and secured approximately 100TB of data stolen from the gang’s victims.

Andy Grote, senator for the interior of the City of Hamburg, said: “This international strike against the KillSec group marks the second international operation in just a few months in which Hamburg’s State Criminal Police Office has played a key role.

“The operation was intensively prepared from Hamburg and coordinated in cooperation with international partners. This demonstrates the strength and effectiveness of Hamburg’s security agencies in combating the most serious forms of cyber crime.

“It also sends a signal to anyone who commits grave crimes while believing themselves safe within the apparent anonymity of the internet,” said Grote. “I thank everyone involved for their tremendous efforts.”

Dutch national

Computer Weekly understands that one of the arrests, made in the UK, was of a Dutch national who was named and indicted today by the US Department of Justice as Foaud Eltibrizi, also known as “Archduke”. He now faces extradition to the US.

“The defendant and his co-conspirators carried out targeted intrusions against multiple companies and organisations, stealing highly sensitive information and attempting to extort their victims for substantial sums of money,” said Héctor Ramírez‑Carbó, acting US attorney for the district of Puerto Rico, where the charges were unsealed.

“Ransomware remains a serious and evolving threat to all sectors of our economy, from critical infrastructure to small businesses,” said Ramírez‑Carbó. “The Justice Department and the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Puerto Rico will continue to work closely with our international partners to identify, disrupt, and prosecute anyone – anywhere – who seeks to harm US and Puerto Rico businesses and consumers through these attacks.”

The identities of the other alleged cyber criminals have not been revealed and additional investigations into other potential gang members continue.

Healthcare and financial services were key targets

According to Singapore-based cyber company Group-IB, which provided behind-the-scenes support during Operation KillSwitch, the KillSec gang – also variously known as Kill Security and k1llsec, emerged in 2024 and rapidly established itself as a significant player in the ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) ecosystem, widely recruiting affiliate hackers.

Group-IB said it had identified at least 274 publicly disclosed victims, with the US accounting for around 35%, Europe accounting for approximately 14%, and the UK for roughly 3%.

Initially favouring Windows environments, KillSec began targeting VMware ESXi hosts in November 2024 as part of a major expansion that also saw it move to increase its share of the ransoms its affiliates garnered.

In general, its attacks followed the “path-of-least-resistance” with victims targeted via phishing, brute-force attacks on exposed Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) services, known vulnerabilities in internet-facing applications, and misconfigured cloud storage vaults. title: Bank of England warns of AI debt
raw_text:
The governor of the Bank of England has issued a warning to investors about the return on investment (ROI) of artificial intelligence (AI).

In an interview on BBC Radio 4, Andy Bailey said: “There is a very large amount of investment going into the AI sector. That’s natural because it’s a major area of growth.”

However, while he believes AI needs financing given its potential to be a major contribution to growth to the UK and world economy, he warned that its contribution may not be as great as financial markets expect and it could take a lot longer to reap those financial benefits.  

His comments come just days after Reuters revealed a leaked prospectus for Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO), valuing the AI firm at $2tn. Bloomberg also interviewed OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, who spoke about the need to get AI safety right before being held accountable to investors, as and when the company eventually goes public.

Responding to a question from Bloomberg about the company’s IPO, Altman spoke about the increased capabilities of frontier AI models and the need to implement AI safety: “While we are going through this period of adjusting to this new level of capability and the new safety requirements, we just want to get our feet under us, make sure we understand how to operate in this new way and be able to make some of these decisions without the pressure of being a newly public company.”

The Bank of England’s Record of the Financial Policy Committee (FPC) meeting of 25 September 2026 reported that developments in AI could affect a wide range of investors and funding markets. The committee noted that an increasing volume of AI-related investment is being financed through debt issuance.

“The increasing indebtedness of AI firms combined with opacity and, at times, ‘circular arrangements’ that can be associated with this financing, can complicate the assessment of risks and could amplify losses if expectations disappoint,” the FPC warned.

The committee also warned that growth prospects and fiscal outlooks are partially dependant on the expectation that AI development and adoption will generate significant productivity gains. The FPC said: “A reassessment of those expectations could therefore affect not only AI-related asset valuations but also sovereign debt markets.”

In addition, the FPC discussed how a narrowing of the current capability gap between open-weight and closed-weight AI model capabilities would make more advanced capabilities widely accessible. This presents a potential AI safety risk as open models could be exploited by cyber criminals, but it also means that advanced AI capabilities are also available to everyone without the premium that is generally associated with the advanced closed models from frontier AI firms.

Clearly, if advanced AI capabilities are available as open models, technology buyers may choose these potentially cheaper models over the most advanced models on offer from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI. In addition, open models tend to require less powerful hardware, which means the token cost of an open model together with the AI acceleration hardware cost are both significantly less than closed models.     

Investors in AI firms may have to wait more than five years before they see any measurable returns, according to analyst Gartner. The analyst firm projected that AI capital investment in aggregate would not achieve a return on invested capital (ROIC) of 12% – the investment hurdle rate – until 2032 at the earliest.

From an IT buyer’s and CIO strategy perspective, there is a very real risk that some of the businesses they have bought AI products from may not be around by then. There is also a risk that AI inference and machine learning costs will rise significantly as publicly listed AI companies look to increase shareholder value and fund continued investments in expensive AI acceleration hardware.

title: NetApp aims Novus storage at AI factory bottlenecks
raw_text:
NetApp used its Insight conference in Las Vegas to unveil Novus, a storage architecture it claims can scale to up to 100TBps of throughput to keep artificial intelligence (AI) factory graphics processing units (GPUs) fed.

Meanwhile, NetApp chief executive George Kurian (pictured) argued that data – not compute – now forms the main constraint on enterprise AI, and presented Novus alongside new European data sovereignty controls, an expanded AI Data Engine and a fresh Oracle partnership.

NetApp said neoclouds and GPU-as-a-service providers build AI factories at a scale legacy storage was never designed for, and that GPU utilisation can fall below 30% when storage cannot feed enough data to the processors.

Novus, he said, separates metadata from the data path so performance, capacity and concurrency scale independently under a single NFS namespace, combining Novus Data Director metadata software on Supermicro hardware with OnTap data services on AFF A90 systems. NetApp said the architecture is available to order now and provides a path to software-defined deployments.

“Data is becoming the constraint to productively scale AI,” said Kurian. “93% of organisations report that at least one form of data challenge is blocking their AI ambitions.”

Kurian put the scale of that challenge in numbers, noting that large language model scale has grown by 5,000 times in four years, and that about 85% of a typical enterprise’s data sits in unstructured form – engineering documentation, research data, media and decades of institutional knowledge scattered across siloed systems. “Petabytes of your unstructured data are dark, with hidden knowledge ignored,” he added.

Syam Nair, NetApp’s chief product officer, framed the launch as an economics problem. “AI factories struggle and GPU economics collapse when data can’t keep up,” he said. “HPC [high-performance computing]-era storage alone cannot serve AI factory scale – the industry needs a true architecture built for it from the ground up.”

Meanwhile, NetApp Keystone Sovereign adds controls beyond data residency, including European-based support and escalation paths, European-controlled access management and clearer documentation of telemetry and data flows, with initial pilots planned for Germany and France.

“Fragmented data, dark data, uneven protection, facing rising attacks and hardening sovereignty rules – this is the state of most customers’ data estates,” said Kurian.

Kurian framed the announcements around what he called the agentic enterprise, in which autonomous software agents act on an organisation’s behalf. Those agents need “memory and context”, he argued, and turning data into trusted, governed context is the job he outlined for the AI Data Engine.

The expanded AI Data Engine lets organisations discover, govern and activate data where it lives without creating copies, with metadata capability that now spans heterogeneous sources beyond NetApp storage. NetApp has made the AI Data Engine free for the first six months, while an expanded Commvault integration aims to detect threats earlier and recover clean data in minutes rather than days or weeks. And a newly expanded partnership makes OnTap storage available on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

Simon Robinson, chief analyst for storage and data infrastructure at Omdia, said data sovereignty is becoming a defining requirement in regulated markets. “Solutions that can provide that clarity while preserving the flexibility of as-a-service infrastructure are well positioned to build trust and expand adoption in sovereignty-sensitive regions,” he said.

title: Microsoft, UAE Cyber Council and Core42 deploy AI cyber defence across government
raw_text:
Microsoft, the UAE Cyber Security Council and Core42 have announced plans to deploy Microsoft’s artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cyber security platform, MDASH, across UAE government entities to strengthen national cyber resilience and accelerate the adoption of secure AI technologies across the public sector.

The initiative will see the three organisations collaborate on the phased implementation of MDASH, an AI-driven cyber security capability designed to help security teams identify vulnerabilities, prioritise risks and improve security posture through automated analysis and advanced AI models.

The deployment represents the latest step in a broader strategic partnership between Microsoft, Core42 and the UAE government, which has already seen significant investments in sovereign cloud infrastructure, artificial intelligence and cyber security capabilities across the country.

According to the organisations, the collaboration aims to give government entities enhanced tools to defend against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats while supporting the UAE’s wider ambitions to build one of the world’s most advanced and trusted digital ecosystems.

“Code safety is a national priority and a cornerstone of cyber resilience,” said Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, head of cyber security for the UAE government. “As AI becomes integral to government and critical services, securing the code that underpins these systems must be built in from the outset, not treated as an afterthought. Bringing MDASH capabilities to the UAE is a major catalyst for wider adoption of AI-powered code security across government and our national digital ecosystem.”

Under the proposed framework, the Cyber Security Council will support the adoption and responsible use of AI-powered cyber security technologies through the UAE’s National AI Test and Validation Lab, helping government entities evaluate and implement emerging cyber defence capabilities.

Core42, a G42 company and Microsoft’s sovereign cloud partner in the UAE, will provide onboarding, implementation and capacity-building services through its Sovereign Public Cloud offering. The company will also support participating organisations with integration services and operational guidance focused on security, privacy and resilience requirements.

The initiative builds on the strategic relationship between Microsoft and G42, one of the most significant AI partnerships in the region. Earlier investments between the two organisations included Microsoft’s multi-billion-dollar strategic investment in G42, designed to accelerate AI development and cloud adoption across the UAE and wider Middle East.

The partnership has already resulted in the launch of sovereign cloud and AI services designed to meet local data residency, privacy and regulatory requirements, enabling government and regulated-sector organisations to deploy advanced AI technologies while maintaining operational control over sensitive data.

“Governments around the world are increasingly looking to AI as a force multiplier to protect the nation, its critical assets and people,” said Hayete Gallot, executive vice-president of security and emerging technologies at Microsoft. “AI can be a powerful tool for cyber security. Together with the UAE Cyber Security Council and Core42, we will help government organisations strengthen resilience, improve cyber readiness and build capacity for emerging threats.”

The deployment of MDASH also aligns with Microsoft’s broader cyber security investments in the region. Over the past several years, the company has expanded its cloud footprint in the UAE while increasing investments in AI, security services and digital-skills programmes aimed at supporting both public- and private-sector organisations.

For Core42, the initiative further reinforces its role as a key enabler of sovereign AI and cloud infrastructure across the UAE. The company has been central to several national AI initiatives and has worked closely with government organisations to deliver secure cloud environments that can support large-scale AI workloads.

“The UAE has made a deliberate choice to lead in AI adoption,” said Talal M Al Kaissi, CEO of Core42. “This collaboration combines world-class AI security capabilities with sovereign infrastructure and local expertise, giving government entities access to advanced cyber defence capabilities while keeping security, privacy and operational control at the centre.”

The roll-out is expected to begin with awareness sessions, pilot programmes, technical workshops and onboarding activities for participating government entities before expanding more broadly across the public sector. The partnership aims to help government organisations strengthen protection of critical services, improve trust in digital systems and prepare for the next generation of cyber threats.

title: Atos invests in AI education for West Midlands youth
raw_text:
Free artificial intelligence (AI) training is being offered to up to 650,000 young people in the West Midlands to help them become AI ready.

IT services firm Atos is investing money into Tech First Youth’s Future Readiness initiative which will see schools and colleges in the region receive free access to resources. It will have a focus on AI discernment, which is the ability to discern when AI outputs should be used or when caution is required.

“By teaching AI literacy and critical thinking, Futures Readiness equips young people and educators to live, learn and work in a world increasingly shaped by AI,” said Atos.

Although AI is a concept dating back decades, the widespread take-up of generative AI (GenAI) began around 2022 with the release of ChatGPT. It was a wake-up call for governments and businesses alike, which must prepare for inevitable disruption. Likewise, seemingly all careers must be tailored to work with AI technology.

Because AI will touch all of society, the programme aims to use the AI training resources across the curriculum rather than as an individual course. “Society and the workplace are being reshaped by AI with new capabilities, risks and behaviours emerging in cycles of weeks and months,” said Atos. “Futures Readiness is designed to help education keep up with the development of AI as responsive enrichment to the curriculum, rather than a static course or one-off intervention.”

Every three weeks, interactive videos will be made available to schools to help them respond to live developments in AI.

Atos has made several commitments to educating the UK’s youth. In October last year Michael Herron, the UK head at Atos said he was “utterly determined” not to allow GenAI to pull up a career drawbridge.

Back then, Herron said Atos’s plans will take into account the increasing use of GenAI. “I am working on this whole model around the coexistence of humans and AI together, because AI can do some people’s jobs,” he said.

“We are redefining the skills the next generation of UK-based talent need to thrive in an AI-driven workplace. We believe these will be both technical and softer skills, such as curiosity, experimentation and creativity.”

As a result, careers will be “multi-dimensional and much more ubiquitous”, he said, adding: “I do not subscribe to the view that there are going to be mass redundancies because of AI and agentic. What I do subscribe to is that there are certain roles which will become defunct, but there will be new roles in the world of agentic.

“There is a sad amount of high youth unemployment at the moment, but I don’t buy into the fact that it’s because the junior jobs are going to go – they’re just going to be different.”

In February, also in the West Midlands, Atos’s first UK apprentices began training to become IT staff of the future as part of its programme to train IT support professionals in the era of AI.

As part of this, Atos’s agentic factory, which will feature AI agents and people working together on customer IT projects, was opened at the supplier’s delivery centre in Solihull, on the outskirts of Birmingham.
